notes.meaning: Israel had no king or national leader at this time, and the people did not honor God as their true King. A Levite, a member of the tribe set apart for religious duties, lived in the hill country of Ephraim and took a concubine from Bethlehem. A concubine was legally recognized as a secondary wife, but she had lower social standing and fewer rights than a primary wife.

differ.view: Some teach that taking a concubine was a clear moral failure against God's creation design for marriage, while others note that the law tolerated concubines even though it was not God's ideal.

notes.meaning: The woman became unfaithful or angry with her husband and returned to her father's home in Bethlehem. She stayed there for four full months before any attempt was made to bring her back.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern interpreters translate the ancient Hebrew root as being angry or departing in disgust rather than committing marital unfaithfulness.

notes.meaning: The Levite decided to pursue her to speak kindly to her heart and win her back. He brought a servant and two donkeys to carry her home. When he arrived, her father was glad to see him, hoping for a peaceful reconciliation.

The father-in-law urged the Levite to stay and enjoy his hospitality. Welcoming guests with generous meals was a sacred duty of honor in the ancient world. The Levite accepted and spent three full days eating, drinking, and resting there.
Early on the fourth morning, the travelers prepared to leave for home. The woman's father stopped his son-in-law and urged him to eat some bread first to build up his strength for the road.
The two men sat down and shared a plentiful meal together. As they visited, the host pleaded with the Levite to stay another night and enjoy more time together.
The Levite stood up to start his trip, but his father-in-law kept begging him to stay. Yielding to his host's strong urging, the Levite agreed to lodge there a fourth night.
Early on the fifth day, the Levite prepared once more to depart. The father again asked him to eat first, and the meal stretched on until the afternoon began to fade.

As the travelers got ready to set out, the host warned that the day was drawing to a close. Ancient travelers normally stopped pitching tents by late afternoon, so leaving then was dangerous. The father begged him to sleep over one more night, but the Levite was ready to leave.

The Levite refused to stay another night because he wanted to get home. He packed his two saddled donkeys and set out with his concubine and servant. By late afternoon, they arrived opposite Jebus, which later became known as Jerusalem.
Daylight was running out as they reached Jebus. Knowing the danger of traveling after dark, the servant wisely urged his master to turn in and spend the night in the city.

The Levite refused to stay in a city belonging to the Jebusites, who were foreign Canaanites. He wanted to avoid staying with non-Israelites, believing they would be far safer among their own people. He decided to keep walking north to the Israelite town of Gibeah.

The Levite encouraged his group to press on as fast as possible to find shelter. He aimed to reach either Gibeah or Ramah before dark. Both towns belonged to the tribe of Benjamin along the northern road.
The group pushed ahead, but the sun sank below the horizon just as they drew near Gibeah. Because darkness made travel risky and difficult, they were forced to stop there for the night.

The travelers entered Gibeah and sat down in the open city square, waiting for someone to invite them in. Towns in those days rarely had public inns, so travelers depended entirely on private hospitality. Shockingly, not a single person in this Israelite town offered to take them in.

At dusk, an old man came into the city after working hard in the fields. Though he lived in Gibeah, he was not a Benjamite by birth, but an outsider from the hill country of Ephraim, the Levite's home territory.
The old man looked up and noticed the travelers stranded in the public square. Seeing that no one had offered them shelter, he asked them where they were coming from and where they were going.

The Levite explained that they were traveling from Bethlehem back home to the hill country of Ephraim. He added that he was going to the house of the Lord, likely the tabernacle at Shiloh. He also shared his pain that no one in Gibeah had welcomed them into a home.

The Levite explained that they would not be a financial burden to anyone who took them in. They had brought plenty of straw and feed for their animals, as well as bread and wine for themselves. All they needed was a safe place to sleep.

The old man gave them a warm greeting of peace and offered to provide everything they needed. He urged them strongly not to sleep out in the town square. Knowing the wickedness of the town, he knew the street was dangerous.

The host brought the visitors inside and fed their donkeys first, following the ancient custom of caring for animals before oneself. The travelers then washed their feet, rested, and shared a meal together.

While they were enjoying their dinner, corrupt and lawless men from the city surrounded the house. They banged loudly on the door and demanded that the Levite be brought outside so they could sexually assault him. This terrible demand showed that Gibeah had sunk into the same evil as ancient Sodom.

The host stepped outside to face the mob and begged them not to do such a wicked thing. He addressed them as brothers in Israel and pleaded with them to respect the protection of his home. He argued that harming a guest was an outrageous crime.

Desperate to protect his male guest, the host offered to send out his own virgin daughter and the Levite's concubine instead. In trying to guard the rules of hospitality, he proposed an appalling and sinful compromise. Scripture records this event to show how deeply the culture had fallen, not to approve of it.

The mob refused to back down, so the Levite seized his concubine and shoved her outside to them to save himself. The men of the town raped and abused her all night long. They finally let her go when dawn arrived.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the ancient text frames the crime mainly as an offense against the Levite's honor and property rather than focusing on the woman's personal trauma.

notes.meaning: At daybreak, the battered woman crawled back to the house where her husband was staying. She collapsed in the doorway and lay there until full daylight arrived.
In the morning, the Levite opened the doors to leave on his journey. He found his concubine collapsed across the doorway with her hands stretched toward the threshold in a final cry for help.
The Levite told her to get up so they could go, but she gave no answer because she had died from the abuse. He lifted her body onto his donkey and started home in silence.
When he arrived home, the Levite took a knife and cut her body into twelve pieces. He sent a piece to each of the twelve tribes of Israel as a gruesome summons demanding national justice.

Everyone who saw the pieces was horrified by the crime committed in Gibeah. They agreed that no evil like this had happened since the nation came out of Egypt. The people called for all the tribes to think carefully, hold council, and take decisive action.
